_comment: Machine-readable index of every preventive control in this repo, and the
defect it exists to stop. This is the memory of the Defect Feedback Loop:
when a BUGS or SEC ticket closes, its root cause is traced to a control
here — either one that already exists (and failed to fire, which is itself
a finding) or a new one that gets added.
Enforced by scripts/check-control-registry.py, which fails the build if a
control's implementation is missing, if it is no longer wired into any
workflow (the SEC-79 'silently disabled for weeks' failure mode), or if a
check script exists in the repo but is not registered here.

controls.name: Workflow integrity check
controls.summary: Static scan for workflow patterns that report SUCCESS while doing nothing — GITHUB_TOKEN pushes that suppress downstream triggers, --limit 1 deploy verification, 401 acceptance without SHA verification, rollback steps that never roll back.
controls.escape_hatch: # integrity-ok:

controls.name: Action SHA-pinning check
controls.summary: Every remote GitHub Action must be pinned to a full 40-hex commit SHA. A mutable @tag lets upstream change CI code without review.
controls.escape_hatch: # integrity-ok: pin

controls.name: Server-action export check
controls.summary: A 'use server' file may only export async functions. Next.js 16+ rejects anything else at action-invocation time; the build does not catch it, so the defect ships green and 500s every form submission.
controls.escape_hatch: // server-action-exports-ok:

controls.name: Service-role client centralisation
controls.summary: The service-role client bypasses all RLS. Its construction is confined to one hardened factory so a hardening change lands once rather than at ~30 call sites.
controls.escape_hatch: // service-role-ok:

controls.name: Routine ownership guard
controls.summary: Asserts the one-concern-one-owner markers survive edits, so probing does not re-quadruplicate across routines and each signal keeps a single authoritative source.

controls.name: Doc mirror manifest presence
controls.summary: Fails the PR if a runbook or compliance doc listed in the mirror manifest has been deleted or renamed out of the tree.

controls.name: Doc mirror content check
controls.summary: Fails the PR if a listed mirror exists but is an empty or stub file — the 'backup that looks successful but contains placeholder content' failure mode.

controls.name: CODEOWNERS single source of truth
controls.summary: GitHub uses only the first CODEOWNERS it finds and silently ignores the rest, so two files means the lower-precedence one's ownership rules are dead.

controls.name: UI/copy founder-ownership guard
controls.summary: Any PR touching a founder-owned UI or copy path must carry a UI-Change-Approved or UI-Bugfix-Only commit trailer.
controls.notes: KAN-474: the script also exposes `--describe`, which emits the founder-owned surface DERIVED from is_protected() itself (parsed from the function body, not restated). The Backlog Autopilot routine reads that at runtime instead of carrying its own copy of the list. Two prior drifts — KAN-415 moving two copy modules, KAN-473 adding src/modules/*.tsx — were invisible to CI because a SaaS routine prompt is not readable from CI, so the fix was removing the second copy rather than adding a third checker. tests/scripts/check-ui-copy-ownership.test.js pins it, including a count ratchet: silently deleting a rule keeps guard and description in agreement, so equality alone cannot catch it.

controls.name: macOS Finder-duplicate file check
controls.summary: Rejects committed ' <n>'-suffixed Finder-copy duplicates, which shadow the canonical module, are never imported, and confuse audits.

controls.name: Auto-heal pattern catalogue self-test
controls.summary: Verifies every auto-fix pattern still matches its fixture and does not false-positive on a sibling — the regression guard that stops the auto-fix workflow silently breaking.

controls.name: Fix-only promote guard
controls.summary: Blocks a production promote whose pending changes are not all bug fixes, under the (now withdrawn) fix-only auto-promote exception.

controls.name: Signup surface gate
controls.summary: Blocks a staging promote that changes a signup-surface path without the corresponding E2E coverage having run.
controls.self_test: npx jest tests/scripts/check-signup-surface-gate.test.js
controls.notes: Armed under KAN-415 D6. This control shipped 2026-07-25 with NO tests of its own, which matters more than it sounds: its own header states the daily Staging Soak deliberately never exercises signup (it reuses a persistent reset-user), so this gate is the only thing proving account creation still works before code reaches staging. The KAN-419 spike then demonstrated that a modularisation move renames the surface out from under the manifest and the gate reports RESULT: CLEAN - exit 0, no warning, no log. tests/scripts/check-signup-surface-gate.test.js now pins both halves: the behavioural contract (fires on the surface, stays quiet otherwise, content-filters migrations, fails closed when unverifiable) and a two-way ratchet asserting every src/ glob in the manifest still resolves to tracked files. Mutation-proven three ways - performing the real D6 move with the manifest untouched reddens 2, disarming matches_glob reddens 12, and turning the fail-closed branch into a CLEAN reddens 1.

controls.name: Backup integrity check
controls.summary: Fails if a backup artefact is a placeholder rather than real data — a dump that does not start with '--', contains no CREATE statements, or is suspiciously short.

controls.name: Complete-backup verification
controls.summary: Asserts the full platform backup contains every expected component rather than a subset that still exits zero.

controls.name: Release drift check
controls.summary: Reports divergence between the environments in the promotion chain so a stale beta cannot make a production promote a silent no-op.

controls.name: Secret rotation reminder
controls.summary: Flags credentials past their rotation interval.

controls.name: Main-chain guard
controls.summary: Fails loud if main gains any commit not present on beta — i.e. a change that did not arrive through develop → staging → beta → main — and blocks any PR targeting main.
controls.escape_hatch: BYPASS CONTROLS commit marker
controls.notes: NOT yet in main's required status checks — see docs/DEFECT_FEEDBACK_LOOP.md open gaps.

controls.name: Dashboard loading.tsx guard
controls.summary: Fails any PR that reintroduces a src/app/**/loading.* without an explicit marker — the Next 16 Suspense boundary that never reveals on hard load and blanks the dashboard.
controls.escape_hatch: // loading-tsx-ok:

controls.name: Manual-of-Me loader coverage
controls.summary: Asserts every known loader of profile_manual_of_me selects the full field allowlist. Superseded in generality by CTL-021 but retained as the incident-specific pin.

controls.name: Partial-write safety
controls.summary: Generalises BUGS-74. Any function that filters a caller-supplied record through an allowlist and writes it must treat `undefined` as 'not provided' (omit) rather than 'clear' (NULL). Function-scoped so a guard in a sibling function cannot launder an unguarded writer. Paired with a runtime contract suite and an auto-discovering loader-coverage test that needs no hardcoded file list.
controls.self_test: python3 scripts/check-partial-write-safety.py --self-test
controls.escape_hatch: // partial-write-ok:

controls.name: Partial-write runtime contract + loader discovery
controls.summary: Runtime assertions that omitted fields never reach the DB payload, that explicit clears still clear, plus a scanner that discovers every reader of a form-backed table (rather than trusting a hand-maintained list) and checks the allowlist against the actual migrated columns.

controls.name: Migration privilege lint
controls.summary: Every migration must revoke a SECURITY DEFINER function from public, anon AND authenticated. Revoking from PUBLIC alone is a no-op on Supabase, which grants anon/authenticated directly via ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES — the first version of this rule required only the PUBLIC revoke and passed a fixture shipping an anon-callable function. That mis-specified revoke in 20260622120000_two_axis_access_model.sql is the actual root cause of SEC-28/29/42/43. Also pins search_path, forbids GRANT to anon, requires RLS on new public tables, and (R5) blocks duplicate migration version timestamps. Ratcheted against a baseline that may only shrink. R6 (BUGS-77, 2026-07-30): every function named by an UNGUARDED REVOKE/GRANT must be CREATEd earlier in the lineage - ordering, not just presence, since a function created in a later migration is still a replay failure. Revokes inside a do-block are excluded because they no-op on a fresh database. Also fixed an R4 false positive: DDL text inside a string literal (an event trigger's 'CREATE TABLE AS' tag list) was read as a real CREATE TABLE.
controls.self_test: python3 scripts/check-migration-privileges.py --self-test
controls.escape_hatch: -- db-privileges-ok:

controls.name: Live database security invariants
controls.summary: Asserts seven invariants against each running database, because migrations are applied with the Supabase MCP tool and therefore reach a database without passing through a PR. INV-2 was replaced 2026-07-27: the original NULL-ACL test was structurally unfireable on Supabase (pg_default_acl forces an explicit ACL, so proacl is never NULL) and reported clean forever; it now detects duplicate SECURITY DEFINER overloads, the real signature-change vector. Missing credentials or an unapplied RPC report UNVERIFIED, never a silent pass.
controls.self_test: python3 scripts/check-db-invariants.py --self-test
controls.escape_hatch: supabase/security-invariants-waivers.json

controls.name: Waiver and escape-hatch hygiene
controls.summary: An escape hatch with no owner and no expiry is not an exception, it is a silent repeal. Every waiver needs ticket, owner, reason and exactly one of expires (fails on lapse) or review_by (notifies). Every in-code bypass marker must cite a Jira key.
controls.self_test: python3 scripts/check-waiver-hygiene.py --self-test

controls.name: Control registry integrity
controls.summary: The meta-control. Fails if a registered control's implementation is missing, if it is no longer referenced by any workflow (the SEC-79 'silently disabled for weeks' mode), or if a check script exists in the repo but is not registered — so the registry cannot drift away from reality.
controls.self_test: python3 scripts/check-control-registry.py --self-test

controls.name: Defect feedback loop coverage
controls.summary: Closes the loop. Cross-references the BUGS/SEC tickets closed each week against the registry and reports any defect fixed without a control behind it, so a fix is never just a repair. Baseline at adoption: 22.5% of 129 closed defects had a control. Driven by the weekly cloud routine, whose runbook is its wiring.
controls.self_test: python3 scripts/defect-control-coverage.py --self-test
controls.escape_hatch: labels: third-party-outage / upstream-bug / vendor-config

controls.name: Suspension-guard coverage
controls.summary: A PUBLIC-SURFACE file may not read the `profiles` BASE TABLE; public surfaces read `public_profiles`, whose view body carries every visibility predicate and therefore applies even to service_role (RLS does not). Default-deny: everything under src/app/ is public unless it matches a short authenticated carve-out list, so a NEW public route is covered the day it is written. KAN-473 added named PUBLIC-FACING MODULE ROOTS after KAN-415 D9 moved five public-profile files out of src/app/ and narrowed the surface 74 -> 69 files — the same quiet-narrowing failure, one commit after the rewrite that fixed it. SEC-104 step 3 replaced the original column-keyed rule, which triggered on the presence of a PARTIAL guard and so could not see an unguarded read at all — and which the SEC-104 migration then blinded completely, taking its public-surface coverage from 4 chains to 0 while its vacuous-pass guard (keyed on a raw count of 2) never fired.
controls.self_test: python3 scripts/check-suspension-guard-coverage.py --self-test
controls.escape_hatch: // suspension-guard-ok:

controls.name: Workflow secret-reference integrity
controls.summary: GitHub expands an undefined secret to the empty string silently, so a workflow can reference a secret that was never created and still report green. deploy-dev.yml had been verifying builds against a blank Supabase config this way. Every secrets.X reference must be in .github/known-secrets.txt (generated verbatim from gh secret list) or in .github/absent-secrets.txt with a reason and a Jira key. Found 7 phantom secrets across 6 workflows.
controls.self_test: python3 scripts/check-workflow-secret-refs.py --self-test
controls.escape_hatch: .github/absent-secrets.txt (reason + Jira key required)

controls.name: Structural dependency rules (module/segment/cycle)
controls.summary: Three structural import rules, enforced so the codebase cannot regress while the modularisation programme (KAN-415) runs: nothing under src/lib/** may import src/app/** (a library owned by a route folder is how the access-transition matrix ended up inside the admin console, KAN-424 Defect 1); one top-level src/app segment may not import another (a cross-segment edge couples two features so neither can be changed or extracted alone); and no import cycles. The precedent for needing a gate rather than a convention is src/modules/platform/deploy-env.ts — built to be the single environment resolver, it never displaced the six inline derivations because nothing stopped new ones being written. Ships at severity warn and flips to error once the outstanding findings clear.
controls.self_test: npx jest tests/scripts/check-dependency-rules.test.js
controls.escape_hatch: None. A violation is a finding: fix the import or move the shared code to src/lib/. DEPCRUISE_SEVERITY is a roll-out dial, not a per-violation waiver.

controls.name: Bash 3.2 portability
controls.summary: Fails any script under scripts/ using a bash-4-only construct (mapfile/readarray, declare -A, ${v^^}/${v,,}, &>>, coproc, shopt -s globstar). macOS ships bash 3.2 and CI ships bash 5, so these work in CI and exit 127 where releases are prepared. staging-soak.sh documented the rule in a comment from day one and two scripts shipped with mapfile anyway, making the whole unit suite unpassable on macOS — a convention without a gate erodes. Comments are stripped before matching so the fix's own explanatory prose does not trip it; that case is pinned in the self-test. Workflow YAML is out of scope by design: inline run: blocks execute only on the runner, so findings there would only ever be allow-listed, and standing noise is what teaches people to wave a gate through.
controls.self_test: python3 scripts/check-bash-portability.py --self-test
controls.escape_hatch: # bash-portability-ok:

controls.name: Dependabot target-branch
controls.summary: Fails the build if any .github/dependabot.yml ecosystem block omits target-branch: develop. The github-actions ecosystem had no target-branch and fell back to the repo default (main), so every weekly Actions bump opened a PR that main-chain-guard.yml (SEC-98) correctly blocks as a chain-bypass attempt — a permanently-red required check on a benign PR, which trains reviewers to stop reading it.
controls.escape_hatch: None. Every ecosystem must target develop so its PRs flow through the develop -> staging -> beta -> main chain like any other change.

controls.name: Extraction Definition-of-Done
controls.summary: Fails any PR that deletes or renames a file under src/ while an artefact that classifies files BY PATH still names the old path: .github/ (signup-surface manifest, CODEOWNERS, workflows), scripts/ guard path-lists, docs/ (incl. the mirror manifest), modules.json and tests/. A glob that matches nothing protects nothing while CI stays green — KAN-419 measured the docs layer at 18% dead path literals before a single file was moved on purpose. Also requires the PR body to answer the two couplings CI can never see (~/lyra-design-system/build.py and the claude.ai routine prompts, neither in any repo CI can read) and to name the covering Playwright project + soak clause, or record 'no coverage' as a finding. Fails closed (exit 2) when it cannot verify.
controls.escape_hatch: EXTRACTION-DOD-OK: <JIRA-KEY> <check-id> on a commit in the PR. Suppresses exactly one named check, requires a Jira key, every active exception is printed on every run, and more than three in one PR emits a ::warning:: that the hatch is papering over drift.

controls.name: Guard-path-drift
controls.summary: Audits the WHOLE registry on every PR: every path pattern in all 18 registered artefacts must match at least one TRACKED file. Companion to CTL-033, which looks only at the current PR's diff. A pattern matching nothing does not fail - it silently protects nothing while the gate keeps reporting green (the SEC-79 shape). Resolution set is `git ls-files`, so a pattern matching only an untracked or gitignored file FAILS, because CI checks out tracked content and the pattern would be inert there. Implements all seven matching syntaxes separately (bash-case, bash-dbl-bracket, codeowners, literal, glob, regex, basename-regex) because collapsing them produces false verdicts both ways - notably bash's '*' crosses '/' while fnmatch's does not, which would report the largest protected pattern in the estate as dead.
controls.escape_hatch: guard-path-ok: <JIRA-KEY> <reason>

controls.name: Env-access ratchet
controls.summary: Freezes the set of DIRECT process.env reads under src/ (72 references across 37 files at 2026-07-29) in env-access-baseline.json and makes it shrink-only: a new file fails, a new variable in an already-listed file fails, and a listed file or variable that has STOPPED being read ALSO fails so the baseline cannot over-state the problem. src/modules/platform/env.ts is exempt by design. Keyed on file plus variable-set rather than line number, so unrelated edits do not churn it. Exists because src/modules/platform/deploy-env.ts proved that creating a canonical resolver is ~10% of the work - all six derivations it was meant to replace are still inline - and only CI retires call sites.
controls.escape_hatch: // env-access-ok: <JIRA-KEY> <reason>

controls.name: Schema-drift ratchet
controls.summary: Diffs the three committed Supabase schemas (src/types/database/{dev,staging,prod}.ts) as semantic facts - column, enum label, function - against a shrink-only baseline at supabase/schema-drift-baseline.json. New drift fails; a baseline entry that has stopped drifting ALSO fails, so the list cannot quietly over-state the problem. Exists because the app compiles against the dev schema while production genuinely lacks the KAN-153 columns, the KAN-143 'draft' visibility label and two functions - so TypeScript asserts prod has columns it does not, and the type system cannot be its own control. Compares facts rather than lines because the generator wraps a 5-label union and inlines a 4-label one, making a line diff report 16 differences for one fact.
controls.escape_hatch: none - add the drift to supabase/schema-drift-baseline.json with a ticket

controls.name: Test-reimplementation ratchet
controls.summary: Flags a test file that names a subject module, defines a function whose name also exists in that module, and never reaches the real module - neither importing it nor invoking it as a subprocess. Two severities: 'vacuous' (subject never reached; nothing in the file can observe the real code) and 'partial' (subject IS reached but the file also keeps a private copy of some of its logic, which can silently diverge). Exists because tests/unit/maintenance-page.test.js reported 19 passing tests for the public maintenance page's email-capture form while asserting nothing about it - stubbing the worker's isValidEmail, isRateLimited and escapeHtml each left all 19 green, so input validation, abuse limiting and HTML escaping were unguarded on a public unauthenticated endpoint. This is the usual 'a control never seen to fail' problem with a twist: the control fired constantly and reported on a copy. Shrink-only ratchet against tests/support/test-reimplementation-baseline.json, failing on new/worsened findings AND on stale ones. Deliberately narrow - generic names (setup, run, main, handler) are excluded, because standing noise is what teaches people to wave a gate through.
controls.escape_hatch: // test-reimplementation-ok: <JIRA-KEY> <reason>

controls.name: Comment-satisfied assertion ratchet
controls.summary: Flags a source-text assertion whose literal or regex is satisfied by a COMMENT in the module it scans. Two severities: 'comment-only' (the string exists nowhere but the prose, so the guard proves nothing today) and 'comment-shadowed' (it exists in the code AND a comment, so the guard passes for the right reason now but would keep passing if the code were deleted). Exists because expect(sitemap).toContain('is_published') was green throughout SEC-100, when suspended members' slugs reached search engines, and because at src/app/dashboard/profile/page.tsx:27 the comment was written to satisfy the scan - deleting all three real data-fetch lines leaves 11/11 green. Gates the modularisation (KAN-415 moves files, and such a guard follows the prose rather than the code). Strips comments PER FILE TYPE - CSS has no '#' comments so #4a7359 is a colour, and .txt has none at all - and attributes each assertion to the subject read in its own test block, because a test file commonly reads a different subject per block. Both of those were false-positive sources in the prototype and are pinned as self-test fixtures.
controls.escape_hatch: // comment-assertion-ok: <JIRA-KEY> <reason>

controls.name: Design re-baseline gate
controls.summary: Requires design/BASELINE.json's baseline_ref to change in the SAME PR that moves a design-bearing file (src/app/globals.css, src/components/**, or any src/app/**/*.tsx). Exists because the Claude Design build loop's source lives in a different, PRIVATE repo (github.com/luisa-sys/lyra-design-system) that this CI cannot read, so the extraction DoD could only ask a human to attest 'EXTRACTION-DOD-DESIGN-SYSTEM: done' - and an attestation satisfied by typing a word is indistinguishable from no control, the same defect shape as a comment-satisfied assertion (CTL-039) one layer up. The concrete failure it covers is KAN-419 5.1: build.py reads globals.css and reconstructs 21 @dsCard previews from page sources, so a move breaks its source pointer loudly but on the founder's machine, hours later, with nothing warning the agent that moved it. SCOPE LIMIT, stated deliberately: this does NOT prove the design system was re-pointed or regenerated - CI cannot read that repo. It proves someone opened it, took its head and recorded it here, raising a false attestation's cost from 'type a word' to 'go and look'. Fires only on relocation (D/R), not edits, because an edit leaves the pointer resolving; widening it would make every extraction PR demand a meaningless re-baseline and drive people to the hatch by reflex.
controls.escape_hatch: Design-Baseline-Ok: <JIRA-KEY> <reason>  (commit trailer; key AND reason both required)
controls.self_test: scripts/check-design-baseline.py --self-test

controls.name: Module manifest integrity
controls.summary: Asserts modules.json against the actual tree via git ls-files: every tracked file under src/ is owned by exactly one module (longest-prefix wins, as in CODEOWNERS), every declared path still exists, and owns.files matches the real count. modules.json is the input to every boundary rule in the modularisation programme - layers, mayDependOn, mustNot, the dependency-cruiser config, the extraction DoD - and nothing validated it. Three defects were live when this was added: client-ip.ts had been MOVED into src/modules/guards/ but never DECLARED there so it stayed unowned (the very gap the moving commit claimed to close); owns.files had drifted on three modules whose paths are DIRECTORIES, profile declaring 35 against an actual 43, because a file added inside a directory never bumps a hand-typed count; and a nested path across two modules read as an ambiguous boundary when it was in fact correct. A module whose declared path no longer exists owns nothing, and every rule written about it is inert while still reading as configured.
controls.escape_hatch: Add the path to UNOWNED_BY_DESIGN in the test, with a comment arguing why it belongs to no module. Deliberately a literal list, never a glob - a pattern would silently adopt whatever lands next to it.
controls.self_test: Mutation-proven 2026-08-09, all four directions: removing client-ip from guards' paths, overstating profile's owns.files, declaring a path that does not exist, and deleting convene's more specific nested path each turn the suite red; the clean manifest is green.

controls.name: Scheduled workflows are actually active
controls.summary: Queries the GitHub API for every workflow's state and fails when one that declares a cron schedule is not active. A DISABLED workflow still has a perfect file on disk, and every other check in this repo reasons about .github/workflows/*.yml as TEXT - check-workflow-integrity.sh greps it, CTL-023 confirms the file exists and that something invokes it, CTL-035 confirms its path literals still match - so all of them pass for a workflow GitHub will never run again, because `state: disabled_manually` lives in the API and nowhere in the repository. Found 2026-08-09: 4 of the 20 workflows declaring a cron schedule were inactive and had been since mid-June, including anomaly-detect on */15. Two things hid it - CLAUDE.md still documented 'Sunday 04:00 Stryker mutation testing' and a Sunday 23:00 staging auto-promote as live cadences, and Dependabot kept bumping all four files (#474), so they kept appearing in diffs looking maintained. This is SEC-79 exactly, and the lesson taken from SEC-79 does not cover it, because existence and invocation were never what broke.
controls.escape_hatch: An entry in .github/scheduled-workflow-exceptions.json carrying BOTH a Jira key and a reason. An entry for a workflow that has since been re-enabled is a STALE exception and fails outright, so the list cannot only grow. BUGS-102 (2026-08-14): this description was ALREADY written this way and was only half true - the exceptions lookup sat behind the `state != active` branch, so it could cover a registered-but-disabled workflow and NEVER an unregistered one. Since GitHub does not register a `schedule` trigger until the file is on the default branch, any PR ADDING a scheduled workflow was failed by the gate its file had to pass to reach that branch - a deadlock with no documented way out. The lookup now runs on both branches, so the hatch matches what this field always claimed. An unregistered workflow with NO exception still fails; a 'not yet registered' entry is expected to be SHORT-LIVED and becomes a build failure as STALE the moment the workflow registers and runs. Still ships WARN-first locally (SCHEDULED_WORKFLOW_GATE_ENFORCE=1 to block, which pr-checks.yml sets).
controls.self_test: 13 cases. Seven cover the parsing decisions, notably that a COMMENTED-OUT cron is not a live schedule (backup-complete.yml ships its cadence commented until commissioning, and reading that as scheduled would raise a permanent unresolvable finding). SIX cover the CLASSIFICATION decision and are net-new under BUGS-102, which is the lesson worth keeping: the original seven all tested declares_cron() and the Jira-key regex, so the judgement this control actually makes had NO fixtures at all and the deadlock lived comfortably in main()'s untested body. classify() was extracted so it could be exercised directly: unregistered+exception -> excepted (the defect); unregistered without one -> FAILS (no regression); exception on a now-ACTIVE workflow -> STALE (the ratchet); registered-but-disabled with and without an exception -> unchanged; and ACTIVE with no exception -> clean, so the others are not satisfiable by a classifier that flags everything. Mutation-proven 2026-08-14, each mutation asserted to have applied: reverting the fix reddens exactly the first case, removing the STALE arm reddens exactly the third. The jest test also gained a FLOOR on the corpus - it matched the passed-count line with a regex whose denominator moves with its numerator, so it caught a fixture that FAILED and never one that was DELETED; gutting the corpus to 2 now reddens 2 tests. Verified live 2026-08-09: warn mode exits 0 naming all four inactive workflows, --enforce exits 1. Re-verified 2026-08-14: 20 scheduled workflows, 2 excepted (BUGS-90, SEC-98), all active.

controls.name: Architecture rules span every library root
controls.summary: Asserts that no-module-to-app's from-path covers every library root declared in modules.json, and every tracked file under each, enumerated from git ls-files rather than sampled. The rule is BLOCKING - library code may not import from a route tree, because that means shared logic is owned by a page (KAN-424 Defect 1). Its anchor read ^src/lib/ until 2026-08-09, when the KAN-415 D1 extraction moved 28 files into src/modules/ - every security guard and every Supabase client among them - and every one silently left the rule's scope. Nothing went red: the rule kept matching the files that had NOT moved, so it kept reporting a clean pass. Proven with a fixture, a src/modules -> src/app edge is an error under the widened anchor and NOTHING under the old one, with identical dependency counts cruised - the edge was seen and discarded. Neither existing control models this: CTL-035 detects DEAD paths and ^src/lib/ still matched 87 files (narrow, not dead), and CTL-033 greps exact moved file paths which cannot match a regex prefix, and sweeps only .github, scripts and docs while this config sits at the repo root. Writing the test also found src/components/ and src/middleware.ts were outside the rule too - widening on a guess would have missed both.
controls.escape_hatch: None by design. If a library root genuinely must be exempt from the boundary rule, remove it from modules.json's declared paths - which is a visible, argued change - rather than narrowing the anchor, which is invisible.
controls.self_test: Mutation-proven 2026-08-09: narrowing the anchor back to the pre-D1 value reddens 3 of the 7 assertions. Fixtures are enumerated from git ls-files, never sampled - a hand-picked list proves the rule covers the paths someone thought of, which is precisely how the original anchor looked correct.

controls.name: Shared-code drift across repos
controls.summary: Compares files that exist as COPIES in lyra and lyra-mcp-server and fails when they diverge. The web app and the MCP servers share rules but no code, so every shared rule is a copy that drifts, and this has already caused a production defect (admin_approve_beta wrote two columns a lyra migration had dropped). lyra-mcp-server/src/convene-recommend-scoring.ts opens by admitting it is a verbatim copy with no mechanism to keep it one. KAN-418 offered two fixes - publish @lyra/contracts, or vendor plus a CI diff. The package was declined 2026-08-09 to minimise supply-chain surface: it would create a path where whoever can publish executes in production on Vercel and both Railway services, and would place read tokens in four runtimes. This alternative costs zero tokens, zero registries and zero runtime dependencies because lyra-mcp-server is public and CI reads it with the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN. It does not remove the duplication; it removes the silence. Found on first run that moderation-policy.ts had ALREADY drifted textually - header comments plus the mandatory NodeNext '.js' import extension - with logic identical, which is why that entry compares normalised.
controls.escape_hatch: Edit shared-code-manifest.json: change an entry's mode from exact to normalised (comments and the NodeNext extension only), or move it to the `deferred` list with a reason. Deferred entries are PRINTED on every run, so a deferral cannot quietly become permanent. An empty shared list fails outright rather than passing vacuously.
controls.self_test: --self-test covers 8 normalisation fixtures, including the two that matter in opposite directions: differing headers plus a '.js' extension must compare EQUAL, while a changed severity comparison or string literal must still differ, and a double-slash inside a string literal must survive. Mutation-proven live 2026-08-09 in three directions: a real change to the exact-mode file goes red, a comment-only change to the normalised-mode file stays green, and a real logic change to the normalised-mode file goes red.

controls.name: Access gate ORDER is a checked artefact
controls.summary: Asserts the access pipelines' exact ORDER, the pairwise invariants that make certain reorderings catastrophic, and that every gate written is wired exactly once. Gate order in src/middleware.ts was a behavioural contract with NO test before KAN-415 D4: whether the suspension gate runs before the beta gate decides whether a suspended user lands on /suspended or /waitlist, and whether SEC-36's 404 runs before authentication decides whether an unauthenticated caller can reach production's oauth_clients. Three instruments, deliberately complementary: exact-order deep-equals catch EVERY change; ORDER_CONSTRAINTS carries the five pairwise invariants as data with tickets and reasons, so a reviewer can tell a cosmetic reordering from a live security regression in seconds; and a registry/ORDER set-equality test closes a failure mode the decomposition CREATES - a gate that exists, type-checks, is unit-tested and never runs. A constraint naming a gate that no longer exists fails rather than passing vacuously on two -1s comparing equal.
controls.escape_hatch: None. Changing an order means editing the expected literal, which is a visible diff a reviewer can weigh against ORDER_CONSTRAINTS' stated reasons. Landed LAST in D4 on purpose: written earlier, every subsequent commit would have edited its own expected list, and in a log that is indistinguishable from weakening it.
controls.self_test: Mutation-proven 2026-08-10. Also guarded at the TYPE level by a dedicated type-level file under tests/types — an @ts-expect-error on assigning an authed gate into a pre-auth pipeline, which fails the build if the error DISAPPEARS. Verified by flipping Gate.run from a property to a method shorthand - property form gives 1 compile error, shorthand gives 0, and the type file then reports TS2578 unused directive. That difference is invisible in review, which is why it is pinned twice.

controls.name: Access gates must not bypass the exemption table
controls.summary: An ESLint no-restricted-syntax rule, scoped to the three gates that consult the exemption table (suspension, beta-tier, admin-host), forbidding direct === / !== comparisons against pathname. Those comparisons are exactly what the table replaced - 19 disjuncts across three inline chains - and a single direct pathname equality comparison added to a gate would bypass it SILENTLY: the table's own tests would still pass, because the table would still be correct; it would simply no longer be the only thing deciding. startsWith stays legal, because /admin needs it and it is the literal qa-sweep/inventory.py derives the admin prefix list from. One legitimate exception exists and is declared at its site: string-building the /admin rewrite for the root path. The plan predicted zero false positives; there is one, and narrowing the selector to allow its shape would also allow a real bypass written the same way, so the exception is declared rather than the rule weakened.
controls.escape_hatch: An eslint-disable-next-line at the specific site, with a comment saying why the comparison is not an exemption decision. Deliberately per-site rather than a selector carve-out.
controls.self_test: Mutation-proven 2026-08-10: adding a direct pathname equality comparison to the beta-tier gate makes npm run lint report the CTL-046 error; reverting clears it. The scoped files contain zero other such comparisons, so the rule fires only on the edit that matters.

controls.name: Documentation Definition-of-Done
controls.summary: Fails any PR that makes a STRUCTURAL change whose meaning is written down - a file added/removed under src/modules/, a workflow added/removed, a control script or the control registry, a migration, or a path-keyed guard manifest - without either touching a doc (docs/**, CLAUDE.md, README.md, modules.json, controls/registry.json) or recording a Docs-Updated/Docs-N/A trailer. The trigger set is deliberately narrow: a gate that fires on every PR is one people learn to wave through, and that reflex defeats every other gate too. It cannot tell whether a doc is TRUE - nothing can - it answers the narrower question 'you changed something that is written down somewhere, did you go and look?'. Fails closed (exit 2) when the diff base cannot be resolved.
controls.escape_hatch: Docs-Updated: <JIRA-KEY> <what changed and where> or Docs-N/A: <JIRA-KEY> <why no doc describes this> on a commit in the PR. Both require a Jira key AND a reason - a bare key does not satisfy it. Docs-N/A is a legitimate answer and not a loophole: recording that you checked IS the review step. What must not happen is nobody looking.
controls.self_test: python3 scripts/check-docs-updated.py --self-test
controls.notes: Built after a 60-agent audit on 2026-08-10 compared every architecture/runbook/plan doc against the real tree. Three confirmed findings would have made a fresh session do the WRONG thing: the modularisation plan still read 'the extraction programme D1-D15 is DEFERRED ... No file moves into src/modules/' four days after that ruling was reversed and with 44 files already moved on main; CLAUDE.md and RUNBOOK.md both described no-module-to-app as covering src/lib/** only, long after the anchor was widened because 28 files had silently left a BLOCKING rule's scope; and RUNBOOK.md called the dependency gate non-blocking two weeks after it was flipped to error. Every one was written by someone who had just done the work and knew the truth - docs do not drift through carelessness, they drift because nothing is watching and the person who would notice already knows.

controls.name: Live schema parity
controls.summary: Asks the three LIVE Supabase databases for their columns and asserts (a) every table present on more than one database exposes the same columns, except where supabase/schema-drift-baseline.json records a ticketed difference, and (b) each committed src/types/database/<env>.ts matches its own database. Exists because CTL-036 - the repo-side half - compares the three committed SNAPSHOTS to each other and therefore cannot see all three going stale the same way, which is the state they were in on 2026-08-11: every snapshot was missing gift_voucher_hint while all three databases had it, and CTL-036 was green. Runs in the promotion chain because a promotion is when a column gap becomes an outage - code written against one schema reaching a database with another. Detects drift in BOTH directions; dev is behind staging and prod on gathering_invite_messages.claimed_at (BUGS-62), so a prod-is-missing-only check would sail past it. Fails closed with exit 2 when a credential is absent rather than skipping. SEC-133: the live-vs-snapshot half ALSO runs daily via db-invariants.yml (--snapshot-only), because running only on a promote meant drift surfaced at the door of a release and nothing looked for it in between. Only that half runs daily: the cross-database half is red for the whole of any staged migration rollout, and SEC-131 proved the snapshot half is the one that matters - all three databases agreed perfectly while all three snapshots were wrong, so live-vs-live was blind to it. Remediation is one command: npm run gen:db-types -- --env <env>. SEC-143 (2026-08-14) extends it to a FOURTH snapshot that lives in ANOTHER REPO: lyra-admin-mcp-server/src/types/database.ts, the copy of prod.ts that BUGS-101 types the admin server's writes against so a dropped column is a compile error. Nothing proved that copy still matched the database - it could rot exactly as the untyped code it replaced did, just in one file instead of many. Run with --with-admin-contract; the cross-repo read uses `gh api` and the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN, the same mechanism CTL-043 uses, so no new secret exists anywhere. It lives HERE rather than in the admin repo for two reasons: SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN would otherwise have to be copied into the repo with the weakest guard estate (SEC-51), and check-control-registry.py requires an implementation file to exist in THIS repo - a checker in the admin repo could not be registered at all, leaving the feedback loop blind to it. Compared BOTH ways: a column the contract declares but prod lacks is the BUGS-101 shape itself; a column prod has but the contract lacks is staleness. The contract is a five-table SUBSET, so a table absent from it is deliberately NOT a finding - treating the subset as drift would make this red on day one forever, and an always-red gate is one someone turns off.
controls.escape_hatch: none - apply the missing migration, or record the difference in supabase/schema-drift-baseline.json with a ticket
controls.self_test: 23 cases via --self-test. The SEC-143 half adds 8, built as snapshot-shaped TEXT so the real parser runs rather than a stub. Mutation-proven 2026-08-14: suppressing the contract-declares-a-dropped-column direction, suppressing the staleness direction, and letting an unparseable contract compare clean each redden it. A fourth mutation - reporting prod tables the contract omits - also reddens, and that is the one that matters in practice, because breaking the subset rule is how this becomes permanently red. \u26a0\ufe0f One mutation deliberately did NOT redden and is recorded rather than hidden: live_prod.get(table) -> live_prod.get(table, set()) still produces findings, one per column instead of one per table. It degrades the MESSAGE, not the coverage - a badly chosen mutation, not a blind spot. Saying so is cheaper than someone re-deriving it later.

controls.name: Migration ledger parity
controls.summary: Asks whether supabase/migrations/ can REBUILD the databases, which is the axis no other database control looks at. CTL-036 diffs the three committed snapshots against each other; CTL-048 diffs each live database against its own snapshot; check-db-invariants.py asks each database for its privilege posture. All three ask 'is the schema right?', all three were green on 2026-08-12, and all three were correct - none of them reads supabase/migrations/ at all. Measured when this landed: of 82 committed migrations, exactly 1 could be identified in dev's ledger by both version and name, 0 in staging, 1 in prod. mcp_tool_call_log and content_moderation_flags are live tables on all three environments whose creating SQL does not exist in version control; several of the other orphans are the June 2026 anon-grant and SECURITY DEFINER revokes, so a rebuild would be insecure in exactly the way the repo appears to have fixed. Production's ledger has no row for create_lyra_schema at all, and add_api_keys is in the repo with a live table on every environment while no ledger records it as ever having run. The failure was invisible because it is not drift BETWEEN environments - those are mutually consistent - but between the running system and its source of truth. Root cause is gotcha #9: apply_migration writes to the database and its ledger but not to the repo, so committing the SQL is a separate step. Two-way ratchet against supabase/migration-ledger-baseline.json: a NEW divergence fails, and a baselined one that has been RESOLVED also fails, so the file cannot become a suppression list. Fails closed on a missing token, a non-200, or an unparseable body. Read-only: DELETE on the same path rolls migrations out of the history table, so the method is hard-coded and asserted.
controls.escape_hatch: none - commit the migration SQL that was applied out-of-band, or apply the migration that was committed; a divergence that is accepted goes in supabase/migration-ledger-baseline.json via --write-baseline, never by hand

controls.name: Audit report readability
controls.summary: Reads the `npm audit --json` report for the weekly security audit and FAILS CLOSED (exit 2) on anything it cannot measure - missing file, empty file, unparseable body, or a document that is not an npm audit report. Exists because both halves of security-audit.yml previously turned a failure-to-measure into a clean result: the workflow's inline `except: print(0)` fed the `if: ... != '0'` guard on its ONLY failing step, so a parse failure SKIPPED the failure and the run passed; and audit-to-email.py's `except` returned has_vulnerabilities:False, which suppressed the alert email. Green tick, no email, nothing assessed - the SEC-79 shape and forbidden pattern #3 (the report must distinguish 0 from fetch-failed). The trigger was mundane: `> report.json 2>&1` merged npm's warnings into the JSON, and with --json npm writes the report to stdout and warnings to stderr, so any warning corrupted it. A third defect in the same block recorded npm's exit code AFTER `|| true`, so it always read 0. Exit 2 is deliberately distinct from 1 (ran, found something) because a caller that cannot tell those apart is how this started. Extracted from an inline YAML heredoc, where nothing could import or test it.
controls.escape_hatch: none - a report that cannot be read is not a clean audit; fix the report or the redirect

controls.name: Module dependency policy (layers, mustNot, mayDependOn)
controls.summary: Enforces the dependency architecture modules.json already declared. Every module carries a `layer`, a `mayDependOn` and a `mustNot`, and the manifest states the policy explicitly - edge src->dst is allowed iff layer(dst) < layer(src) or dst is in declaredSameLayer[src], with upward edges FORBIDDEN ABSOLUTELY. Nothing read any of it: all 21 modules carried "enforced": false and no script or test consumed that field, so the manifest described an architecture rather than constraining one. Three rules, deliberately independent so that renumbering a layer cannot silently legalise an edge another declaration forbids: (1) the layer rule; (2) `mustNot`; (3) `mayDependOn` - KAN-415 C2's no-undeclared-module-dep, which catches what rule 1 structurally cannot, since a DOWNWARD edge is legal at every layer and without it any module may quietly acquire a dependency on any lower one. Measured across the 62 cross-module edges: 12 violate the layer rule or mustNot; 50 are declared in mayDependOn, 9 sit in mayDependOnCandidatesPendingDecision and are reported as a distinct `pending-decision` kind (the manifest's own record that the question is open, as against plain drift), and 3 were declared nowhere. Before touching the graph it judges the MANIFEST against itself and refuses to proceed on a contradiction - a grant the layer rule overrides is not a permission but a comment, and trust-safety.mayDependOn held exactly one: `admin`, an L3->L4 edge the same file calls forbidden absolutely, simultaneously listed as an open question. Contradictions are NOT baselineable and --write-baseline refuses to launder one, because a baseline records an accepted violation OF the policy and an incoherent policy has nothing to violate. Module-level cycles (access<->admin, admin<->trust-safety, age<->auth, profile<->recommendations - invisible to depcruise's file-level no-circular) are covered by rule 1 rather than a fourth rule: each is one legal downward edge plus one upward edge already flagged. Deliberately not a dependency-cruiser rule - the policy is a function of JSON fields across 21 modules, which as regexes would be ~400 generated pairwise rules going stale on every layer change; depcruise still produces the graph, this classifies it. Two-way ratchet with a third arm: a NEW violation fails, a baselined one that has been FIXED fails as stale, and a baselined edge that starts violating for an ADDITIONAL reason fails as CHANGED - `kinds` is part of the comparison, so a newly-added rule cannot arrive pre-suppressed on every edge already listed. Fails closed (exit 2, distinct from 1) on an unreadable manifest, an empty or unparseable graph, or a missing baseline.
controls.escape_hatch: none - move the shared code down a layer, or declare the dependency in modules.json if the architecture is what changed; an accepted violation goes in modules-layering-baseline.json via --write-baseline, never by hand. A manifest contradiction has NO escape hatch at all: fix modules.json.

controls.name: npm-audit gate, scoped and waiver-aware
controls.summary: SEC-105. `npm audit --audit-level=high` ran FULL-TREE at five blocking sites - pr-checks plus all four deploy workflows - while the production dependency tree had 0 vulnerabilities at every severity and 973 of 1249 resolved packages were dev-only. It was also the only gate in the estate keyed on a THIRD-PARTY FEED rather than on Lyra's own code: every other control can only be tripped by a change in the PR, this one went red overnight on an unchanged repo when somebody else published an advisory. In deploy-production.yml it sat in `lint-and-unit-tests`, a transitive `needs:` ancestor of the deploy job, so a rescore killed the release before any other step ran. The cost was paid in unshipped security fixes: SEC-88 froze the pipeline ~11 days with 40+ CI-green PRs queued and twelve tested security fixes left live-vulnerable in every environment, across six outages in five weeks (SEC-89/90/91/92/94/97). The gate also manufactured risk - SEC-94's blanket brace-expansion pin crashed `npm run lint` and needed three nested scoped overrides to work around. This control replaces it: prod-tree scoped, blocking, in pr-checks ONLY; removed from all four deploys, which re-audited a lockfile the PR gate had already passed (every tree reaching them arrived via a PR, per SEC-98 + main-chain-guard) and so added no information and one spontaneous-failure window; full tree still audited weekly by security-audit.yml, which now opens or updates a labelled GitHub issue rather than only emailing. NOTE `--omit=dev` is NOT 'what ships' - npm's split is a DECLARATION, and minimatch/brace-expansion/fast-uri reach the prod tree via @sentry/nextjs bundler plugins and postcss via next, all build-time tools that never execute in the serverless runtime; it is a far better risk proxy than the full tree, not a clean runtime boundary. An unfixable advisory is a decision, not a bug: security/npm-audit-waivers.json carries advisory + package + severity + ticket + owner + reason and a dated `expires` that FAILS the build on lapse (fails CLOSED, unlike Snyk, whose docs concede a malformed expiry persists indefinitely). A waiver names ONE package and does not transfer to another package sharing the advisory. Waivers are two-way: one matching nothing is STALE and fails - asserted only under --scope full, the run with complete information, since a prod-scope run cannot see a dev-only advisory and only warns. Fails closed (exit 2, distinct from 1) on empty output, unparseable JSON, an npm error envelope, or any document lacking metadata.vulnerabilities - 'no findings' and 'no measurement' must not look alike, which is SEC-136. SEC-140 (2026-08-14) — BOUNDED RETRY ON TRANSIENT FAILURE ONLY. Because this gate reaches a third-party registry it is the one control here that can go red with NO change to the PR, and it did: an unreachable registry returned an npm error object with an empty summary and detail, the gate correctly refused to call that clean, and a PR with 3830 green tests was blocked. The same tree audited clean minutes later with only a docstring changed. That is recurrence SEVEN of the class in SEC-101's root-cause table (SEC-89/90/91/92/94/97); SEC-105 had fixed the blast radius and left the class. run_audit now retries up to AUDIT_ATTEMPTS with backoff, but ONLY for network-shaped failures - the process failing to launch, empty stdout, and the npm error envelope - each tagged retryable=True at its raise site rather than matched on message text, because a message-matched retry would silently begin retrying a real finding the day someone reworded a string. A deterministic failure (unparseable JSON, missing metadata.vulnerabilities, npm<7 format) is NOT retried: three attempts would spend minutes reaching the identical answer, and a gate that is slow for no reason is one people learn to skip. Exhausted retries STILL exit 2 - a retry that gave up and reported clean would be strictly worse than no retry. The fix is deliberately not 'make the gate advisory': a production tree needs a blocking audit, and switching off a control that fired for the wrong reason is this estate's single most-repeated mistake. The retry notice is routed through a `notify` seam rather than printed directly, because the self-test's own transient fixtures were annotating the run summary of EVERY green PR four times over. Four standing ::warning:: on a passing build is how people learn to scroll past warnings, which is the same erosion that lets a switched-off control keep looking fine (SEC-79). The self-test collects the notices and prints one summary line instead, and the jest layer asserts BOTH that the line reports a non-zero count (the loop ran) and that a green run emits zero ::warning:: (no standing noise).
controls.escape_hatch: security/npm-audit-waivers.json - advisory + package + severity + ticket + owner + reason and exactly one of `expires` (fails on lapse) or `review_by`, governed by CTL-025. Empty is the correct steady state. There is no hatch for a prod-tree HIGH that has a fix available: fix it.
controls.self_test: Mutation-proven 2026-08-13: a prod-tree HIGH blocks; a MODERATE does not; a matching waiver clears; a waiver does not transfer to another package or another advisory; a stale waiver fails under --scope full and warns under --scope prod; an unparseable report exits 2; re-adding npm audit to a deploy workflow, unwiring the PR gate, and removing the weekly issue each turn the suite red. SEC-140 added 9 cases and they were mutation-proven at BOTH layers, which is how a real defect in them was found: the block was first inserted AFTER the self-test's `if failures:` check, so all eight assertions appended to a list nothing read. Removing the retry, making exhausted retries report clean, and making deterministic failures retryable ALL still passed. Moving the block above the check made every mutation red - three self-test cases for the first, one each for the others - and the jest layer catches the same removal in three of its twenty. The jest test asserts the retry WARNINGS appear during --self-test, so it measures that the loop ran rather than that its cases exist.

controls.name: No deep module imports (declared API surface)
controls.summary: KAN-415 C2 `no-deep-module-import`. CTL-051 constrains WHICH modules may depend on each other and says nothing about which FILES a permitted dependency may reach, so a consumer could import any file of any allowed module. Measured when this landed: 304 files across 21 modules, of which only 54 are imported from outside - the other 250 were internals in fact and public in policy, and any of them could acquire an external consumer with nothing going red. That gap is the difference between a module and a directory. Asserts that every import crossing a module boundary lands on a file listed in the target's `declaredApi`. TWO-WAY, and the second half is the point: a declaredApi entry nothing outside the module imports is STALE and fails, so the public surface RATCHETS DOWN rather than only growing - without it declaredApi would be a suppression list. Seeded from measurement (the 54 real crossings) so it ships at zero violations, which is not circular: a control red on the day it lands is one someone turns off, and the value is forward-acting - the next deep import fails and the fix is either to route through an existing entry point or to add a reviewed line to modules.json. Plan 4.5 prescribes exactly this basis, an API of 'the symbols measured as consumed, not what looks tidy'. Deliberately NOT tsconfig aliases: KAN-432 established that an alias only governs imports written in alias form, so a relative specifier (../../modules/x/internal/thing) resolves and type-checks regardless - aliases catch the honest mistake and miss the shortcut. Reading the resolved graph sees both, and needs no index.ts to exist (there are none; creating 21 plus their aliases would rewrite every import in the app for enforcement this provides directly). Has NO --write mode on purpose - regenerating policy from observation would mean every deep import legalises itself on the next run and the gate could never fail; --suggest prints and a human commits. Fails closed (exit 2, distinct from 1) on an unreadable manifest, a manifest with no modules, or an empty/unparseable graph.
controls.escape_hatch: add the file to that module's `declaredApi` in modules.json - by hand, reviewed. There is no marker and no baseline: widening a module's API should be a visible decision, not a suppression.
controls.self_test: Mutation-proven 2026-08-13. Removing the sanitise entry from the guards module's declaredApi turns its real consumers into DEEP imports (exit 1). Declaring a genuinely-internal convene file - precondition asserted, not assumed - fails as STALE (exit 1); the first attempt at that proof picked an already-declared file, so the byte-level 'mutation applied' check passed while the intended condition was never created. --suggest leaves modules.json byte-identical. An empty graph exits 2.

controls.name: Edge-safe middleware bundle
controls.summary: KAN-415 C2 `edge-safe`. src/middleware.ts runs in the Edge runtime, which is not Node: no fs, no crypto module, next/headers is a Server Component API that throws there, and the full @supabase/supabase-js client is the wrong one (@supabase/ssr is the Edge-safe path and is what the middleware uses). The hazard is that NOTHING IN THE IMPORT CHAIN ANNOUNCES ITSELF AS EDGE CODE - a gate file three or four hops from middleware looks like any other module file, so adding a Node-only import to it breaks every request through the gate pipeline, at request time, on a deployed environment rather than at build time. Asserts that no file transitively reachable from an edge entry point imports a banned specifier: any node: builtin, the classic bare builtins, next/headers, and @supabase/supabase-js. Measured when it landed: 23 files reachable from middleware.ts importing exactly three external packages (@supabase/ssr, jose, next/server), all Edge-safe - zero violations, so it ships blocking rather than baselined. Scoped to the REACHABLE SET, not the repo: node:crypto is perfectly legal in Node-runtime code and src/modules/age/didit.ts uses it today, so a repo-wide scan would be red on correct code. A banned list rather than an allowlist, because an allowlist fails on every legitimate new package and a gate that fires on legitimate work is one people learn to wave through. Comments are stripped before matching (CTL-039): this script's own docstring names every banned specifier, and a scan that punished writing the explanation down would be pointed the wrong way. VACUITY GUARD: fewer than 8 reachable files exits 2, because a traversal that silently reached nothing reports zero findings and a green tick, indistinguishable from a clean bundle. Fails closed (exit 2, distinct from 1) on an unusable graph, a missing or renamed entry point, or a collapsed bundle.
controls.escape_hatch: none - use an Edge-safe equivalent (@supabase/ssr, Web Crypto, NextRequest headers) or move the work out of the middleware's import chain. There is no marker: a Node-only API in the edge bundle is not a style question.
controls.self_test: Mutation-proven 2026-08-13: a node:crypto import added THREE HOPS from middleware, in an ordinary-looking gate file, turns the check red (exit 1) and names the file and line; a graph where middleware reaches nothing exits 2 rather than reporting clean; an entry point absent from the graph exits 2; and a banned import in a file OUTSIDE the bundle correctly does not fire.

controls.name: Module table ownership
controls.summary: KAN-415 SS4.3. `modules.json` has carried an `owns.tables` / `owns.rpcs` list for every module since the manifest was written, and until this landed NOTHING READ THEM - 242 non-`profiles` `.from()`/`.rpc()` call sites against an ownership map no code consulted. An ownership map that nothing enforces is documentation, and documentation describing a boundary is indistinguishable from an enforced boundary right up until someone crosses it. Asserts that every database call sits in a module that declares the table it touches. THE POINT IS THAT IT SEES WHAT CTL-051 AND CTL-053 CANNOT: those constrain the IMPORT graph, this constrains the DATA graph, and Convene is the proof they are different boundaries - it is the best-contained module in the estate (2 declared entry points, every outward edge legal and downward, both enforced two-way) and still reaches 3 tables owned by other modules. TWO-WAY RATCHET on supabase/table-ownership-baseline.json: the 56 pairs present at landing are grandfathered so it ships green (a control red on day one is a control someone turns off), a NEW pair fails, and a baselined pair that has been FIXED fails as STALE so the list can only shrink. The baseline COMPUTES a `_concentration` field at write time rather than carrying a typed number, because 29 of the 56 pairs come from one file - the account erasure/export path, which touches every table a user has data in by definition - and without that figure the baseline reads as 56 boundary breaks and invites a cleanup that would be wrong. `profiles` is EXCLUDED BY POLICY, not omission: it is co-owned at COLUMN granularity (8 modules, 37 of 42 columns, zero bogus claims) with no module owning the table, so table-granularity enforcement would flag all 68 of its call sites; and COLUMN-granularity enforcement was considered and rejected because it cannot be done honestly in static analysis - 6 of 18 `profiles` writes pass a variable rather than a literal, so a gate covering the other 12 would report clean over exactly the shape BUGS-74 was. That contract is pinned at runtime by tests/unit/partial-write-safety.test.ts instead. Reads TRACKED state via git ls-files, never a disk walk, because `git mv` leaves the source directory behind empty. Commented-out calls are skipped (CTL-039) so the prose explaining a removed access cannot re-create the finding. VACUITY GUARD: fewer than 60 call sites exits 2, because a detector that has stopped matching reports zero violations and a green tick, indistinguishable from a clean estate. READ/WRITE CLASSIFICATION (2026-08-14): `owns` means 'may WRITE', so a cross-module READ is legitimate and a cross-module WRITE is the real boundary break. Measured: 44 read, 12 write. Without the split the baseline is a flat list of 56 'boundary breaks' of which 44 are fine, and demanding a ticket and expiry on all 56 - which KAN-415 criterion 2 asks for literally - would be a renewal ritual, which is how a ratchet decays into a suppression list. THE THIRD FAILURE MODE, ESCALATED, is what the first cut could not see: a pair is keyed `module -> table`, so a baselined READ that quietly became a WRITE kept its key, the pair count did not move, and the control stayed green - a module beginning to mutate state it does not own with nothing going red, which is the BUGS-74 shape. De-escalation (write -> read) fails as STALE too, so the record follows the code both ways. AN UNDECIDABLE STATEMENT IS CLASSIFIED `write`, NEVER `read`, and that direction is the whole design: a write misfiled as a read sits in the accepted bucket where it can never be caught escalating, because it was already a write; an over-flagged read costs one annotation. The `basis` field records HOW each verdict was reached - `mutation-call` (hard evidence: a literal .insert/.update/.upsert/.delete), `rpc-undecidable` (the function body is SQL, not in this import tree), `opaque-builder` (the builder was assigned to a variable and mutated elsewhere, which static analysis cannot follow). Of the 12 writes, 7 are mutation-call and 5 are conservative; `account -> search_by_contact_hash` is provably `return query select` in supabase/migrations/ and is a deliberate over-flag. Labelling it matters because a list of 12 'boundary breaks' containing one unexplained false positive is a list people stop trusting.
controls.escape_hatch: Two, both visible and reviewed: add the table to that module's `owns.tables` in modules.json (a one-line diff a reviewer can weigh), or record the pair with `python3 scripts/check-module-table-ownership.py --write-baseline`. controls.name: Route thinness (app-routes-are-thin)
controls.summary: KAN-415 criterion 2 names nine dependency rules. Eight are enforced (two by depcruise, four by CTL-051/053/054, and platform-is-a-leaf plus backoffice-not-in-request-path fall out of CTL-051's layer model). `app-routes-are-thin` was the ninth and was NEVER BUILT, because 'thin' was never defined. Measured at landing: 99 route-ish files under src/app (page/layout/route/*actions), 48 of them making 217 direct database calls, LOC median 102 and max 1060. DEFINED AS A RATCHET, NOT AN ABSOLUTE. 'A route makes no direct database call' is the right end state and the wrong gate: it is a 48-file, 217-call relocation programme - precisely the work criterion 3 concluded was unnecessary once CTL-055 could assert table ownership WITHOUT moving files - and a rule that reddens 48 files on day one is a rule someone turns off, which this estate has six documented instances of ending badly. So the direction is stated and the movement is enforced: the count may only shrink. KEYED PER FILE, NOT A TOTAL - a single aggregate would let one file improve while another regressed and net out to green, the same blindness CTL-055 had before ESCALATED. NOT a duplicate of CTL-055: that asks whether the module owns the table (the data graph), this asks whether data access happens in a request entry point at all (where code lives); a call can pass CTL-055 and fail here. ⚠️ ITS PATTERN IS DELIBERATELY NOT CTL-055's. Borrowing the quoted-identifier regex undercounts silently: it misses supabase.storage.from('profile-files') (7 real sites, hyphenated bucket names) and .from(someVariable) entirely. This matches any .from/.rpc call and excludes the JavaScript builtins by receiver - Array.from and Buffer.from appear 8 times in these files and are not database calls. Excluding by receiver rather than argument shape is what lets it stay loose enough to catch a dynamic table name.

Two cases pin the pattern traps specifically: Array.from and Buffer.from must NOT count, and a hyphenated storage bucket plus a variable table name MUST. Mutation-proven 2026-08-14: removing WORSE detection, removing NEW detection, dropping the builtin exclusion, and counting commented-out lines each redden the self-test. Proven on the real tree too - appending one supabase.from('profiles').select() to src/app/api/health/route.ts turns the gate red as NEW, exit 1.

controls.name: Production release is tagged
controls.summary: Asserts main's HEAD carries a release tag, checked from OUTSIDE promote-to-production.yml. That workflow can finish green with `Create release tag` SKIPPED: a deploy parked on the SEC-106 required-reviewer gate is treated as terminal (deliberately - failing it once fired a spurious auto-rollback on 2026-07-31, run 30666194572, which then died on a Vercel 409), so the promote exits 0 with deploy_state=awaiting-approval and the tag job never runs. It prints 'skipped, not passed' and names the remedy; nothing checked that anyone performed it. Measured 2026-08-14: SEVEN of the last fourteen production releases are untagged, and every untagged one postdates the reviewer gate landing on 2026-07-30 - so for two weeks `git describe --tags`, the authoritative version here because package.json drifts (gotcha #12, BUGS-89), was wrong for about half of production with nothing red. Deliberately a DETECTOR of the end state rather than a change to the promote's exit condition: BUGS-97 proposes failing the wait step, but auto-rollback is `if: failure()` over `needs: [verify-source, smoke-tests]`, so getting that wrong reintroduces a spurious production rollback - worse than an untagged release. States BUGS-97's own principle: a workflow cannot be the only witness to its own completion.
controls.escape_hatch: None, and deliberately none. The remedy is to create the missing tag by re-running promote-to-production.yml once the deploy has completed - a release that cannot be identified is not a state worth suppressing. The only latitude is --grace-minutes (default 40), which covers a promote that has merged but not yet reached its tag job; inside that window the check WARNS and exits 0, and says so, rather than skipping silently.
controls.self_test: 10 cases via --self-test, each driving the real script as a subprocess against throwaway git repos so `git tag --points-at` is genuinely exercised rather than stubbed (CTL-038). Covers: a tagged head passes; a YOUNG untagged head warns and exits 0; an OLD untagged head (forced with --grace-minutes 0) FAILS and names both BUGS-97 and the remedy; a tagged head still passes at grace 0, so the gate is not always-fire; an unresolvable ref exits 2 rather than reporting clean; and --report refuses an empty corpus instead of printing '0 untagged' (catalogue failure mode 4). That fail-closed case caught a REAL bug in the first draft: `git rev-parse bad-ref` exits non-zero but ECHOES THE REF NAME, so a truthiness check accepted 'no-such-branch' as a SHA and reported a missing branch as an untagged release - a finding invented from a typo. Fixed with `rev-parse --verify <ref>^{commit}` plus a 40-hex assertion. Proven against reality 2026-08-14 rather than fixtures alone: green on the live main branch at v0.1.97, and RED on c8662fbe (the untagged 2026-08-13 release, 824m old).

controls.name: A CI finding describes the failure it actually had
controls.summary: db-invariants.yml's ledger-parity job raised its finding under a bare `if: failure()`, so EVERY non-zero exit printed the divergence story - 'the repo and a database no longer agree ... someone applied SQL that was never committed ... commit the migration SQL'. On 2026-08-14 the dev project returned HTTP 403 and the check exited 2, which means 'I could not read a ledger' and says nothing whatever about agreement. The annotation nonetheless sent the reader hunting for an uncommitted migration that did not exist, on three separate days. That job's own header explains why this matters: it is SEPARATE from the `invariants` job precisely because 'a finding that describes itself wrongly is how an operator learns to skim the annotations'. The handler was doing the exact thing the job was split up to avoid. The compare step now publishes its exit code and the handler branches: exit 1 keeps the divergence text, exit 2 gets a 'could not READ' message that explicitly warns the reader OFF looking for a missing migration, and anything else gets a third branch saying the guidance does not apply - without that fallback a broken interpreter would produce a red run with NO annotation, which reads as infrastructure noise. The script's HTTP error now carries the response BODY. `exc.reason` for a 403 is the literal string 'Forbidden', and this endpoint has two 403 sources needing opposite responses: Cloudflare bot protection (transient; the User-Agent header exists for it) versus Supabase refusing the token's scope (not transient). They are told apart ONLY by the body. ⚠️ Numbered 059 rather than 058: SEC-141's branch had already claimed 058 for the promote concurrency guard. Both branches computed 'next free' from develop, which carried neither, so the registry validator - which reads one working tree - could not see the collision. When two controls are in flight at once, check the sibling BRANCH, not just the merge base.
controls.escape_hatch: none - a wrong finding is worse than no finding.
controls.self_test: 9 cases. Comments are STRIPPED before every source-text match, and that was not defensive writing: the `set +e` assertion failed on first run because the run block's own comment says '`|| rc=$?` rather than `set +e`' - CLAUDE.md catalogue failure mode 2, hit while writing the test for it. Mutation-proven 2026-08-14: reverting the handler to unconditional divergence text, dropping the exit-code output, and swallowing the failure each redden the suite. ⚠️ A FOURTH mutation initially did NOT redden it - deleting `{detail}` from the raised HTTP message passed, because the test asserted `exc.read()` and 'body:' appeared ANYWHERE in the file and the code computing them was left intact above the raise. The parts existing is not the same fact as the parts being used. The assertion now targets the raise expression itself and the mutation reddens it.

controls.name: Promote workflows are serialised
controls.summary: The three promote workflows declared no `concurrency` block, so two runs of the same promote could execute simultaneously. Observed 2026-08-14: a single workflow_dispatch of promote-staging-to-beta produced TWO runs 63 seconds apart. Each promote fetches, merges and pushes, so two in flight sit in the classic lost-update window - one can push over the other's merge, or a promote can act on a ref the sibling run has already moved. That day the outcome was harmless only because someone was watching the run list and cancelled the duplicate by hand, which is not a control. The duplicate dispatch is the SYMPTOM and its cause is unconfirmed - a client retry on a slow 204 is the leading hypothesis, and GitHub's dispatch API is documented at-least-once rather than exactly-once. Chasing the cause is the wrong instinct: the guard makes the cause irrelevant, and covers every future source of a double fire including a human double-click. Each workflow gets its OWN group via `promote-${{ github.workflow }}` - staging to beta and beta to main target different branches and are genuinely independent, so a shared literal group would only make a release slower without making it safer.
controls.escape_hatch: None. In particular `cancel-in-progress` may not be flipped to true - that is the reflexive choice and is actively worse here, because it would kill an in-flight promote MID-MERGE OR MID-PUSH, a nastier failure than the race it prevents. With false the second run queues, then finds the merge already done and no-ops harmlessly. A future edit to true would read as a tightening and would likely be waved through at review, which is exactly why a test holds it rather than a comment alone.
controls.self_test: 9 Jest cases. The workflow corpus is DISCOVERED by globbing promote-*.yml rather than hand-listed, so a fourth promote workflow landing tomorrow is covered on arrival; the first case asserts the discovered corpus is exactly the three known files, because every other case iterates it and an empty corpus would report clean while checking nothing (catalogue failure mode 4). Assertions parse the YAML rather than grepping text, so a commented-out concurrency block cannot satisfy them (catalogue failure mode 2). The load-bearing case is cancel-in-progress being false, not merely present. A fifth case pins the REASONING in each workflow file - if someone deletes the explanation they lose the argument for the value, so the explanation is part of the contract. Mutation-proven 2026-08-14 and the mutation was not hypothetical: the first commit on this branch shipped the test and this registry entry WITHOUT the three workflow edits, and CI turned all nine cases red with `concurrency.group: undefined`. GAP, stated rather than hidden: scripts/check-control-registry.py rule 4 sweeps the scripts directory (the check-*.sh and check-*.py globs) and requires every control script it finds to be registered, but it has no equivalent sweep for controls implemented as TEST FILES. This entry was lost once (a `git stash pop` restores the working tree but not the index) and the registry check stayed green throughout, because an unregistered test-kind control is invisible to it. The test itself still ran and still guarded the workflows; what was missing was the feedback-loop memory.

controls.name: SAR export covers every person-keyed table
controls.summary: exportUserData() answers a UK-GDPR Art.15/20 request, and deleteAccount() relies on FK cascade to erase every person-keyed table. The two drifted, and the test that existed to stop exactly that drift (tests/unit/sar-export-completeness.test.js) hard-coded an 18-entry list copied from the export itself, so it discovered nothing from the schema and could only ever agree with the code it was checking. Proven by mutation in both directions before the fix: ADDING a table to the export left it 24/24 green, so the additive direction held no opinion at all. The failure mode is the dangerous one - no query errors, so no export_incomplete_errors key is emitted either, and an incomplete response is indistinguishable from a complete one to both the member and the operator. The replacement derives the person-keyed set by scanning src/types/database/prod.ts for seven person-keying columns and asserts a non-empty corpus floor (> 20) BEFORE iterating, because a derived list that silently comes back empty registers zero tests and reports green. Deriving rather than listing is what found the true scale: 14 tables were missing, not the 9 the ticket named.
controls.escape_hatch: none for the assertion - a table that genuinely must not be exported goes in DELIBERATELY_EXCLUDED in src/modules/contracts/person-keyed-tables.ts with a written reason (the live-credential oauth token tables, and moderation_logs under its ON DELETE RESTRICT Art.17(3)(b) retention).
