controls.name: Routine run-logs carry fresh evidence
controls.summary: Asserts that the newest dated row in each of the three routine run-logs is within that routine's own cadence budget, where the budget is READ from the watchdog registrations already published in docs/OPS_ROUTINES_CONTROL_ROOM.md rather than invented here; a routine with no registration is reported as unmeasurable, never guessed. THE POINT IS THE QUESTION IT ASKS. Every other routine control asks 'did the routine run?' - the Confluence heartbeat, scripts/routine-watchdog.sh, CTL-042's workflow-liveness check. Not one asked 'did its output survive?'. Throughout SEC-146's ten-day gap all of them were correct and green, because the routines WERE running; the evidence simply never reached the repository, since all ~24 run-log PRs were opened as DRAFTS and a draft cannot auto-merge or be merged until a human marks it ready. It lives in the repo rather than inside a routine deliberately: a check a routine performs on its own output dies with that routine, which is the SEC-79 shape one level up, and the repo log is also the copy that survives a wiki incident (BUGS-100 wiped the Control Room page on 2026-08-13 while the repo mirror was ten days stale). NOT WIRED INTO pr-checks BY DESIGN: this control goes red with the passage of TIME rather than the contents of a diff, so in the PR gate it would fail every unrelated PR the moment a routine missed a day - the shape that froze the pipeline for about 11 days under SEC-88 (gotcha 23) and the shape of a gate someone switches off. FRESHNESS IS max(date), NOT the last row: the three logs disagree on ordering (two append at the bottom, one prepends at the top) and DAILY_SECURITY_CHECK's tail is genuinely out of chronological order, so a positional parser would need three rules and still be wrong. Re-sorting those rows to suit a parser would be editing dated measurements while claiming to tidy them - an earlier backfill attempt did exactly that and was thrown away. A row dated D is read as evidence produced at the END of day D, the most generous instant the cell supports, so the control cannot invent a finding out of intra-day timing nobody recorded; the stated cost is that a daily routine may be about a day and a half quiet before this fires, against a defect that was ten days wide. The only price of max is that one forward-dated row would hold the control green indefinitely, which is why a row dated after today is itself a finding.
controls.escape_hatch: None by annotation, and deliberately none. A stale run-log is fixed by landing the missing rows on develop, oldest first, with each row's original date and content preserved verbatim. The only latitude is the cadence budget itself, and that is not editable here - it is read from the Control Room mirror, so widening it is a visible change to the document the watchdog also reads, not a quiet edit to a checker.
controls.self_test: 28 cases via --self-test, each driving the real scripts/check-run-log-freshness.py as a subprocess against a synthetic tree, so parsing, budget lookup, wording and exit codes are exercised together rather than stubbed (CTL-038). Three cases pin hazards the real documents actually contain and a reasonable parser gets wrong: a BLANK LINE inside the table (which per CommonMark terminates it, so an AST parser sees a fresh log as eight days stale), an out-of-order tail (read by max rather than by position), and a decoy first table (the run-log is never the first table in any of the three files). Others pin the fail-closed half: a missing log, a log that is not a regular file, a renamed table header, a table with no dated rows, a missing Control Room, a Control Room carrying no registrations, an unregistered routine, and two registrations disagreeing about one routine. Two cases assert the exit 1 and exit 2 vocabularies stay DISJOINT, per CTL-059 - 'I could not check' and 'I checked and it is stale' are different claims and must not read alike. MUTATION-PROVEN 2026-08-14 against the real documents with 33 assertions, restoring each time: deleting the ten August rows from docs/DAILY_SECURITY_CHECK.md reproduces SEC-146 and turns it red at exit 1 naming 2026-07-28; removing a log, replacing one with a directory, and renaming a table header each give exit 2 with the fail-closed wording and never the stale wording; and both defects at once exit 2 while still printing both findings. THE FIRST MUTATION WAS TOO WEAK AND SAID SO: aging only the newest row left the second-newest inside a 30h budget, so the control correctly stayed green - a one-row edit cannot age a 41-row log, and a mutation that applies is not the same as a mutation that is sufficient.

controls.name: the publish write stays on a credential the user cannot wield
controls.summary: SEC-112: profiles.is_published was writable by any authenticated user straight at PostgREST (table-level UPDATE grant to authenticated, 'Update own profile' RLS with a NULL with_check, no trigger on the column), bypassing publishProfile() and therefore the KAN-408 provider age gate. The fix is a BEFORE UPDATE trigger refusing any is_published change from a JWT-bearing caller. The trap this control guards is that the trigger and the code change are only safe TOGETHER: publishProfile() used createClient(), the anon key carrying the end user's session JWT, so the legitimate publish and the attack were the SAME credential. The trigger alone would have refused the real publish flow in every environment - the BUGS-60 shape, and exactly what the ticket's original implementation plan would have shipped, since it asserted the publish path was already service-role and it was not. So the write moved to createServiceRoleClient(), scoped by the server-validated user id. This test asserts BEHAVIOUR - which mocked client receives the update - rather than scanning actions.ts for the factory name, because the file now carries a long comment explaining the fix and a source-text scan of it would be satisfied by that prose (CTL-039 / gotcha #29). Anyone who 'tidies' the write back onto the user client reddens it. Mutation-proven: reverting that one line turns 2 of 5 cases red. The other half - that the trigger is actually RUNNING on each database - is INV-9 under CTL-024, because a migration reaches a database via the Supabase MCP without passing through a PR.
controls.escape_hatch: none. If the publish write must ever leave the service-role client, the trigger has to be dropped in the SAME change or publishing breaks with 42501 - that coupling is the point, not an inconvenience to route around.

controls.name: Ops-heartbeat Confluence page-id guard
controls.summary: Two Control Rooms are trivially confusable. 33554434 is the Backlog Autopilot Control Room, which has a section called 'Run ledger' of its own; the ops-routines Heartbeat / Run-ledger table that the routine-watchdog reads lives on the other page, 34275370. docs/OPS_ROUTINES_CONTROL_ROOM.md cited the Backlog Autopilot page as the heartbeat source, so an agent following the doc literally lands on the wrong page and either reports '-' for every routine (watchdog UNVERIFIED across the board) or reads the autopilot's Run-ledger rows as heartbeats - a FALSE PASS from the one control that detects a silently-dead routine. Three rules: R1 every mention of the autopilot page id must have 'Backlog Autopilot' within 200 chars; R2 a strong heartbeat-pointer phrase within 60 chars of it is a violation; R3 the anchor doc must state the ops-routines page id within 60 chars of such a phrase, so DELETING the correct pointer fails too rather than only substituting a wrong one. R2's first cut used the wide window and spared any match where the correct id also appeared in it; mutation proof killed that version - repointing the single line 'Heartbeat / Run-ledger table lives on ...' left the guard GREEN because the disambiguation prose two lines up bought the exemption. That mutation is pinned as a --self-test fixture and again as a sandbox case in the jest wrapper, applied to the real doc rather than a synthetic string. Windows are measured in characters across the file, not per line: a line-scoped first draft false-positived on three real files whose 'Backlog Autopilot' wraps to the previous line, and markdown decoration is normalised for the same reason. The phrase list is deliberately narrow ('heartbeat ledger', not bare 'heartbeat') so the registry row reading 'out of scope for the ops-heartbeat' and the docs-ledger row narrating this very defect both stay green - standing noise on the file that documents the fix is how a gate gets waved through. Two false-positive shapes were found by CI, not by the self-test, and both are now pinned as fixtures: R1 taken literally ('only ever named alongside Backlog Autopilot') flagged eleven correct sentences in docs/DAILY_SECURITY_CHECK.md - run-log rows written BY the Daily Security routine while working around this very defect, e.g. 'read from <correct id>, NOT the <wrong id> the prompt names'. R1 now also accepts naming the correct id in the same breath, because contrasting the two IS disambiguation; a sentence naming neither still fails. R2 gained exactly one exemption, an explicit negation inside the tight window, because '<wrong id>, which has no Heartbeat table' is the opposite of a pointer. Both mutations were re-run after the change and both still go red, the one-line repoint via R2. This is the KAN-167 rule applied to the guard itself: a control that fires on the prose documenting its own defect teaches people to wave it through. FINAL SCOPE, after a third CI round: R1 (mere disambiguation) runs estate-wide; R2 (the semantic 'is this a pointer' rule) runs ONLY on the pointer doc, docs/OPS_ROUTINES_CONTROL_ROOM.md. R2's question is only meaningful in a doc that tells an agent where to read; in a narrative run-log the correct sentence is a report OF the defect, and the Daily Security routine appends one on every run - so R2 estate-wide is permanently red or permanently annotated, which is the same thing as switched off. STATED GAP, recorded rather than hidden: if a doc other than the pointer doc starts pointing the heartbeat at the wrong page, only R1 covers it, and R1 is satisfied by naming the correct id nearby. Accepted - the realistic re-introduction vector is an edit to the pointer doc (exactly what BUGS-81 was) or to the stored routine prompt, which is outside the repo and which no CI check can see. The scoping has its own fixtures so that 'R2 fires' and 'R2 fires anywhere' stay distinguishable if POINTER_DOCS is ever widened. 20 self-test cases.
controls.escape_hatch: # heartbeat-page-id-ok: <JIRA-KEY> <reason> on the same line as the id. Intended for text quoting the original defect verbatim, never for a live pointer.

controls.name: No committed script pushes to a release branch
controls.summary: Fails any PR in which a TRACKED file under scripts/ runs `git push` to main, beta or staging. SEC-98 says production changes only via develop -> staging -> beta -> main; that rule lived only in CLAUDE.md while the repo shipped the promote-to-production and promote-to-staging wrappers, which between them held SIX direct pushes - three of them --force onto main - plus a next-step banner advertising staging -> main, skipping beta entirely. Both scripts are deleted by the change that adds this control; the control is the half that stops them returning, because a documented convention with no gate erodes (the staging-soak.sh mapfile lesson, gotcha #28). NO EXTENSION FILTER, and that is the ticket's own lesson turned into code: SEC-99 §1 declared the scripts unreferenced on the strength of a grep over *.md, *.yml, *.json and *.sh, and missed docs/lyra-project-reference.jsx, which presented both of them to a human reader as this repo's promote commands - a signpost to the bypass, which is worse than dead code. So every tracked file under scripts/ is read whatever it is named. MATCHING IS BY TOKEN EQUALITY, NOT SUBSTRING: a fixed-string match for `git push origin main` fires on check-workflow-integrity.sh:194, where that text sits inside a grep PATTERN - a control that detects the defect, misread as the defect - so a line counts only when a `git push` is followed by a token that, after quote-stripping and refspec resolution, is exactly a release branch. That also catches the evasions a fixed string misses: -f, HEAD:main, develop:staging, +main, refs/heads/beta. STATED GAP: .github/workflows/ is deliberately not scanned, because the three promote-*.yml workflows push to release branches legitimately and CTL-016 governs them; nothing outside scripts/ is covered.
controls.escape_hatch: None by annotation, and deliberately none. Most controls here take an `# xxx-ok: <JIRA-KEY>` marker; under SEC-98 there is no legitimate direct push to a release branch from a committed script, so an annotation would be a suppression list for the one behaviour the control exists to forbid - and the real exception process is a two-step human gate in CLAUDE.md, which by definition is not a thing a script does. The supported path is `gh workflow run promote-*.yml`. If this ever false-positives, the fix is a narrower rule in the checker, visible in a diff.
controls.self_test: 56 cases via --self-test, each driving check() against a real temporary git repository so tokenising, comment-stripping, file discovery and exit codes are exercised together rather than stubbed (CTL-038). 15 violating forms (bare, --force, -f, quoted, trailing semicolon, HEAD:main, develop:staging, +main, and a fully-qualified ref, indented, trailing comment) are each asserted twice - caught AND with the right branch named. 12 clean forms are pinned, six of them REAL LINES from scripts/check-workflow-integrity.sh and scripts/rollback-vercel.sh that a substring matcher fails on. Six cases prove there is no extension filter; one proves nested directories are scanned; one pins that untracked files are out of scope; one pins that .github/workflows/ is out of scope; two assert the fail-closed path uses the exit-2 vocabulary and not the exit-1 one (CTL-059 - 'I could not check' and 'I checked and it is broken' are different claims); one asserts every finding is reported rather than the first; and one runs the checker against this repository's own tree, so the checker becoming a violation itself is caught. NOTE ON THE FIXTURES: the violating lines are assembled from a `_PUSH` constant rather than written as literal text, because literal fixtures would make the checker violate its own rule - the CTL-061 failure, where a guard fired on its own registration prose. Assembling them keeps this file genuinely IN scope, scanned with no exclusion and no annotation. MUTATION-PROVEN 2026-08-14, four mutations, each reverted, each asserted to have actually applied first (the KAN-415 D7 lesson - a sed that matches nothing produces a green run indistinguishable from a green run). (1) Restoring the real deleted production promote wrapper verbatim from develop turns it red at exit 1, naming lines 77, 106 and 154 - exactly the line numbers SEC-99 §1 records. (2) Appending one `git push origin main --force` to the real scripts/rollback-vercel.sh turns it red at exit 1. (3) Neutering scan_line to always return None fails 18 of 56 self-test cases. (4) Dropping comment-stripping fails 2 cases, both false positives on documentation lines. ONE PARTIAL RESULT KEPT HONEST: removing the fail-closed precondition entirely (`if False:`) still exits 2, because the empty-tracked-corpus branch catches a missing scripts/ as a second line of defence - so that mutation is detected by the WORDING assertion (1 case) rather than by the exit code. The two paths overlap; only the message distinguishes them.

controls.name: required status checks are still satisfiable, and live protection matches the committed expectation
controls.summary: SEC-106: a required status check is a STRING. GitHub stores the context name a branch demands and never verifies that anything still produces it, so renaming main-chain-guard.yml's `guard` job - a JOB ID, because that job carries no `name:` field - un-gates SEC-98 production change control with no error anywhere: protection keeps waiting for a check nothing reports, the PR waits, and on a repo where enforce_admins is off it is admin-merged and forgotten. THE POINT IS THE QUESTION IT ASKS. CTL-026 proves a control's file exists and something invokes it; CTL-042 proves its workflow is not disabled. Neither proves it BLOCKS anything, because 'the job runs' and 'the merge cannot happen without it' are facts stored in different places - one in the repo, one in GitHub's branch-protection settings. TWO ARMS ON PURPOSE. --local compares .github/expected-protection.json against the jobs this repo defines; it needs no credentials, is decided entirely by the diff, and therefore blocks in pr-checks.yml from day one. --live compares the file against GitHub's real configuration; it needs administration:read and runs on a schedule, because a pull request cannot change branch protection and putting a third-party API on the merge path is the shape that froze the pipeline ~11 days under SEC-88.
